strengths: Addresses an important problem: correcting unreliable LLM planning knowledge through environmental interaction rather than treating generated plans as ground truth.
The proposed components are intuitive and complementary: ADL revises dependencies, FFOM uses operation-level outcomes, and DEX prioritizes apparently achievable unexplored items.
Evaluation includes both embodied MineRL and controlled MC-TextWorld experiments, deliberately perturbed dependencies and operations, component ablations, and detailed per-task results.
The reported results are promising, especially the strong MC-TextWorld graph accuracy and MineRL success on several diamond and gold tasks using a 7B open-weight model.
weaknesses: The central characterization as learning "from scratch" is misleading. Initialization uses human-written plans for an iron sword, golden sword, and diamond, which collectively reveal most of Minecraft's core progression through wood, stone, iron, gold, and diamond—including the headline late-game goals.

Baseline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. ADAM and DECKARD are materially adapted by removing or replacing defining mechanisms, while several task-success numbers are copied from prior work using different models and implementations. Consequently, Table 1 does not isolate the benefit of REPOA.

The claimed efficiency contribution is inadequately validated. There is no direct DEX ablation against random or frontier selection while holding the rest of REPOA fixed, and MineRL learning still uses 400 episodes of up to 36,000 steps and substantial compute.

Important experimental reporting is incomplete: the number of MineRL learning seeds is unspecified, Figure 1 has no uncertainty estimates, statistical significance is absent, and evaluation episode counts vary sharply across tasks. Redstone tasks receive as few as 3–19 trials, versus roughly 30–60 for most others.

There is an apparent sign inconsistency in FFOM. The paper sets x0=-2 but defines invalid operations by n_succ-n_fail <= -x0; this classifies every unseen operation as invalid initially and conflicts with the interpretation of x0 as a failure threshold. The exact implemented rule must be clarified.

The evaluation simplifies the purportedly realistic setting through automatic high-level crafting/smelting, modified ore spawning, and a hard-coded MC-TextWorld controller. These choices are understandable for isolating planning but weaken claims about realistic open-world agents.

The oracle appendix omits golden_sword despite defining six Gold goals, raising questions about the reported aggregate oracle result. Learned REPOA also obtains zero success on every Redstone task and many Iron/Armor tasks, so the broad task-mastery claims are overstated.

Generality is narrow: both testbeds implement essentially the same Minecraft item-dependency system, and the conflict tests alter only a small set of recipes or operation labels. Evidence that the heuristics transfer to other open-world domains or substantially different dependency structures is missing.
No code or artifact-release commitment is provided, and several consequential implementation details and stopping/evaluation procedures remain unclear, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with pseudocode, prompts, hyperparameters, compute estimates, and per-task results provided in the appendices. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/7fc88cb51d5a4052a96059c5ff2315bc/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The paper addresses an important problem: correcting unreliable model-generated planning knowledge through environmental interaction.
The decomposition into dependency revision, failure-aware operation memory, and difficulty-based exploration is intuitive and practically motivated.

Experiments cover both text-based and embodied Minecraft environments, and the knowledge-conflict variants are useful stress tests. The learned system reports substantial gains on several gold and diamond tasks using a 7B open-weight model.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning planning knowledge “from scratch” is overstated. Initialization uses three detailed human-written plans for an iron sword, golden sword, and diamond. Collectively, these explicitly reveal most of the technology progression through wood, stone, iron, gold, and diamond, including quantities and operations. This privileged seed knowledge is especially relevant to the late-game successes emphasized by the paper.

The baseline comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. ADAM and DECKARD are materially adapted: ADAM loses its expert curriculum and starting inventory and instead explores randomly, while DECKARD's original learned policies are replaced by a different operation-memory mechanism. These altered systems may be substantially weaker than the published methods. Table 1 additionally mixes newly obtained results with numbers copied from prior work using different planners and system components, making the claimed overall superiority difficult to attribute to REPOA.

The claimed efficiency contribution of DEX is not directly ablated. Figure 3 studies FFOM and dependency revision, while Table 2 studies dependency knowledge, FFOM, and CRe. Comparisons against RAND or modified prior systems simultaneously change multiple components, so they do not isolate whether DEX is better than random, frontier-based, breadth-first, or uncertainty-based exploration under an equal interaction budget.

There is a serious specification inconsistency in FFOM. The paper defines an operation as invalid when n_succ−n_fail≤−x0, but reports x0=−2. Consequently, an unseen operation with difference zero is already classified as invalid, and an operation needs more than two net successes to become valid. This conflicts with the stated interpretation of x0 as a failure tolerance and leaves the actual implementation unclear.

Statistical reporting is inadequate for the strength of the claims. The number of MineRL learning seeds is not stated, Figure 1 has no uncertainty bands, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. Per-goal evaluation counts vary from 3 to 58, making some estimates extremely unreliable. The oracle evaluation also appears incomplete: golden_sword is absent from Table 12, and the reported Gold average matches the remaining five tasks despite the claimed 67-task evaluation.

The learned system remains brittle: it obtains zero success on every Redstone task and on numerous Iron and Armor tasks. Reporting a macro-average over seven groups gives small groups such as Gold disproportionate influence and obscures this incomplete task coverage.

The robustness tests are narrow, manually constructed perturbations in a deterministic text environment. They closely match the method's fixed operation enumeration and analogy assumptions, and do not establish robustness to noisy observations, stochastic recipes, cycles, changing dynamics, or substantially different open-world domains.

The method relies on strongly Minecraft-specific structure: a known DAG formulation, named inventory items, exact inventory-difference feedback, three predefined operations, atomic crafting and smelting, and explicit success signals. These assumptions limit novelty and generality relative to the broad claims about open-world embodied agents.

Reproducibility remains limited despite detailed appendices: there is no code or artifact release statement, essential sampling/decoding settings and random seeds are missing, and the reported experiment requires roughly 61 aggregate GPU-days. Overall, the work contains promising heuristics, but the confounded evaluation and unsupported central claims prevent it from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: learning planning dependencies through interaction while remaining robust to inaccurate LLM knowledge.
REPOA combines adaptive dependency revision, failure-aware operation memory, and targeted exploration in a coherent framework. The mechanisms are intuitive and technically plausible.
Evaluation spans both text-based and visually grounded Minecraft environments, includes deliberately knowledge-conflicting variants, and shows strong gains over dependency-learning baselines.

The learned system achieves notable performance on difficult Gold and Diamond tasks using a relatively small open-weight 7B model. Component ablations support the value of dependency revision and failure-aware memory.
The appendix provides algorithms, prompts, hyperparameters, per-goal results, compute costs, and an appropriate discussion of limitations and broader impacts.
weaknesses: The claimed contribution of difficulty-based exploration is not isolated experimentally. There is no direct DEX ablation or controlled comparison against alternative exploration strategies, despite efficiency being a central claim.

Comparisons with prior long-horizon agents are not fully controlled: several results are imported from prior work using different planners, while the dependency-learning baselines are materially adapted. This limits attribution of the reported overall advantage.

The claim of learning from scratch is overstated because the method receives all 67 target item names, three detailed human-written plans—including advanced gold and diamond trajectories—and an LLM-generated dependency graph.

There is a reproducibility-critical inconsistency in FFOM: the paper sets x0=-2 but defines invalid operations using nsucc-nfail≤-x0. As written, every untried operation is initially classified as invalid, conflicting with the accompanying explanation and intended behavior.

MineRL statistical reporting is incomplete: the number of learning seeds is unclear, Figure 1 lacks uncertainty estimates, and some per-goal evaluations—especially Redstone—use very few episodes. The substantial compute requirement and absence of a clear code-release commitment further constrain reproducibility.

Scope remains narrow and several learned-dependency task categories contain systematic zero-success goals, so evidence for general open-world applicability beyond Minecraft-style deterministic dependency graphs is limited.
